opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the basic issue is that a failure doesn't really tell you how long the task takes. When we're baselining, we're trying to estimate something like "how long would it take a competent person with the relevant expertise to do this?" If someone succeeds, the time they took is a fairly direct measurement of that. It's noisy, sure, but it's the quantity we care about.

When someone fails, there are many possible reasons, and most of them aren't about the task's inherent length. Maybe the baseliner didn't have the right background. We try to match people to tasks, but it's imperfect, and someone strong in one area of software engineering can still hit a domain they don't know. Maybe they got stuck on an environment issue, or misread the instructions, or just gave up because they were tired or it wasn't worth their time given how we paid them. In all of those cases, the time they spent before stopping is some kind of lower bound at best, and often not even a meaningful one. Someone who quits after twenty minutes because they realize they don't know the library hasn't told you the task takes more than twenty minutes in any useful sense.

There's also a selection question. We care about the time for someone who can actually do it, because that's the comparison point for an AI agent that succeeds. Mixing in failed attempts would blend "how long does this take" with "how likely is a random baseliner to have the right skills," which is a different thing.

That said, conditioning on success has real downsides, and we've thought about them. It biases estimates downward for harder tasks, because the people who succeed on a hard task tend to be the faster, more capable ones. You lose the slow tail. So for the longest tasks we're probably underestimating somewhat, and for some tasks with no successful baselines we had to fall back on researcher estimates. I don't think it's a perfect methodology. But between the options, successful-run times are much closer to the thing we're trying to measure, and failures add more noise than signal.

r001.rationale: The response says successful-run time is a fairly direct, if noisy, measurement, while failures have many possible causes unrelated to task length.

r002.rationale: It mentions that payment can affect whether someone gives up, but does not say success bonuses encourage abandoning a task to seek other tasks they are more likely to complete.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the basic asymmetry is that a success is a pretty strong existence proof, and a failure usually isn't. If someone actually completes a task, that tells you a lot: the task is doable, it's doable with roughly the tools and context we gave them, and here's a concrete amount of time it took. The information is fairly clean.

A failure is much messier. When a person doesn't finish a task, there are so many possible reasons that have nothing to do with how hard the task is intrinsically. Maybe they didn't understand the instructions. Maybe the environment was set up wrong, or a dependency didn't install, and they spent four hours on that. Maybe they just weren't a great fit for that particular task, even if they were a reasonable fit on paper. Maybe they got bored, or ran out of the time we'd allotted, or they decided it wasn't worth pushing through. For a lot of these tasks we're giving people something that's pretty contrived relative to their actual job, so motivation and context effects are real.

So when you see a failure, you kind of have to ask, "Is this telling me the task is hard, or is this telling me something about this particular attempt?" And it's often really difficult to disentangle those from the outside. Whereas if someone succeeded in, say, six hours, I'm pretty confident this is a task that a competent person can do in roughly that range. It might be an underestimate if they got lucky or happened to know exactly the right thing, but at least it's grounded.

There's also a selection issue on our side. We're often writing tasks for which we don't actually have a great prior on difficulty, and the baselining process is partly how we calibrate that. If a task gets zero successes out of a few attempts, the honest answer is often "we don't know how long this takes," rather than "this takes more than eight hours." So treating failures as if they gave you a clean lower bound on difficulty can be pretty misleading.

That said, I don't want to overstate it. Failures aren't useless. If you have a bunch of qualified people try something and they all fail in similar ways, that's genuinely informative, and you should update toward the task being hard or possibly broken. It's more that any individual failure is noisy, and the noise tends to be in a direction that inflates apparent difficulty, so I weight them less when I'm trying to put a number on how long something takes.

r001.rationale: It says success is a strong existence proof with relatively clean information, while failures have many possible causes and are harder to interpret.

r002.rationale: It mentions boredom and deciding not to continue, but does not say success bonuses incentivize abandoning a task to pursue other tasks more likely to be completed.

astra-6.text:
A successful attempt tells you that there exists a way to do the task, and it gives you some upper bound on how much effort it takes. If someone solves a problem in an hour, you know that at least that person, with their background knowledge, can solve it in an hour.

A failure is much harder to interpret. If someone spends an hour and fails, maybe the task requires two hours, maybe it requires a hundred years, or maybe they just tried the wrong approach. You need a much stronger model of how good that person is at finding solutions before you can infer much from their failure. So failures are evidence, but successes tend to give you a more concrete constraint on task difficulty.

r001.rationale: The response says failures are harder to interpret and that successes provide a more concrete constraint on task difficulty.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss success bonuses or people abandoning tasks early to pursue tasks they are more likely to complete.

sol-6.1.text: A successful attempt tells you that the task is possible with the resources and abilities that person had. A failure is much harder to interpret. Maybe the task was too difficult, but maybe they used the wrong approach, misunderstood something, or just didn’t spend enough time on it. So there’s an asymmetry: success gives you a fairly clear upper bound on how difficult the task can be, whereas failure doesn’t give you a similarly clear lower bound. You need more assumptions about how good the attempt was before you can draw that conclusion.

r001.rationale: It says success provides a fairly clear bound on difficulty, while failure has several possible explanations and is harder to interpret.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss success bonuses or people abandoning tasks to seek tasks they are more likely to complete.
